Pathology of Blood Vessels I: Arteriosclerosis PTH LEC · LE 2 · Trans 4A · Socorro Cruz-Yañez, MD, FPSP

Lesson at a Glance

This lecture covers Pathology of Blood Vessels I, with arteriosclerosis (“hardening of the arteries”) at its center.

  • It starts with a review of blood vessel anatomy, the diseases of blood vessels and the vascular anomalies.
  • It explains the vascular response to injury: endothelial cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, endothelial dysfunction / activation and intimal thickening (neo-intima).
  • Its main focus is atherosclerosis.
    • Associated diseases, risk factors, pathogenesis (the response to injury hypothesis), morphology (fatty streak → atheroma) and complicated lesions
  • It ends with the other types of arteriosclerosis: Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis, fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia and arteriolosclerosis (hyaline and hyperplastic).

Most Important Must-Know Concepts

❗ Must Know
  • Fatty streak is the precursor lesion of atherosclerosis.
  • Atheroma / fibro-fatty plaque / fibro-lipid plaque is the basic lesion of atherosclerosis.
  • Atheroma: focal intimal plaque with a central core of lipid and a covering fibrous cap.
  • Predilection:
    • Abdominal aorta
    • Coronary artery
    • Popliteal artery
    • Descending thoracic aorta
    • Internal carotid artery
    • Arteries of the Circle of Willis
  • Key features: modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors → atherosclerosis development and progression → complications:
    • Calcification
    • Rupture
    • Hemorrhage
    • Embolization
    • Aneurysm

A. Review of Anatomy and Blood Vessels pp. 1–3

Arteries Should Know

  • Arterioles
    • Smallest segment of the arteries
    • Provide peripheral resistance to blood flow
    • Have significant effect on blood pressure
  • Majority of the disease of the blood vessels involve the arteries
  • Certain types of diseases have predilection for certain types of arteries
Table 1. 3 Main Types of Arteries
Large / Elastic arteriesMedium Sized / Muscular / Distributing arteriesSmall arteries / Arterioles
  • Medial layer is made up largely of elastic fibers.
  • Allows these vessels to expand during systole and recoil during the diastolic phase (property needed to propel blood towards the smaller arterial vessels and into the tissues).
  • Ex. Aorta and its great/large branches (Carotid and Brachiocephalic arteries)
  • Have thick, circumferentially arranged smooth muscles in the middle layer.
  • Act as a blood pressure regulator through vasoconstriction and vasodilation mediated by the ANS.
  • Ex. Renal, Coronary and Cerebral arteries
  • Measure < 2 mm in diameter.
  • Has a developed smooth muscle middle layer.
  • Principal pathways providing resistance to blood flow

3-Layer Histologic Organization

LayerLecture description
  • Intima
  • (Tunica Intima)
  • Innermost layer
  • Lined with a single layer of endothelial cells with an underlying sub-endothelial collagen and ECM supporting tissues
  • Plays a significant role in the etiopathogenesis of hemostasis, inflammation and cardiovascular pathology
  • Media
  • (Tunica Media)
  • Composed of either: bundles of elastic tissues in large arteries or bundles of smooth muscles in muscular arteries and arterioles
  • Separated and bounded by layers of internal and external elastic lamina
  • Medial layer of muscular arteries and arterioles: well-organized, concentric layers of smooth muscle cells
    • Muscular arteries regulate blood flow and blood pressure through vasoconstriction and vasodilation mediated by the ANS
  • Medial layer of large elastic arteries (aorta and its great vessels): greater amount of elastic fibers
  • Adventitia
  • (Tunica Externa)
  • Outermost layer (lies external to the medial layer)
  • Loose / supporting connective tissues containing nerves, small lymphatics and the vasa vasorum
    • Vasa vasorum: minute blood vessels that provide nourishment / the blood supply of the blood vessels
  • Helps anchor the vessel to the surrounding tissue
Lecture-Specific Note
  • Structurally, all 3 types of blood vessels are organized into 3 distinct layers (Tunica Intima, Tunica Media, Tunica Externa) with some important differences.
  • Some diseases distinctly and preferentially affect certain portions of the vascular wall, making the pathogenesis and morphological patterns of injury unique for that disease.

Veins, Lymphatics and Capillaries

Veins Should Know

  • Larger lumen with large volume capacitance
  • Enclosed with thinner muscular wall
  • Poorly defined internal elastic membrane and poor surrounding soft tissue support
  • Responsible for conducting blood to the heart

Lymphatics

  • Small vessel networks that lie parallel to the arteries, lined with a special type of endothelium with a much thinner muscular wall support
  • Drain lymphatic fluid and inflammatory cells back to the bloodstream
  • Play a role in infection and cancer metastasis dissemination

Capillaries Should Know

  • Very tiny vessels, 7–8 µm (equivalent to the size of an RBC)
  • Connect the arterial and venous channels
  • Network of thin-walled vessels lined by a single layer of endothelium devoid of a media
  • Large cross-sectional surface area with slow flow rate, conveying blood from the arteries to the veins
  • Medium of exchange for diffusible substances:
    • Water
    • Oxygen
    • Carbon dioxide
    • Nutrients and minerals
Table 2. 3 Types of Capillary Endothelium
Continuous endotheliumDiscontinuous endotheliumFenestrated endothelium
Structure
  • Continuous endothelial lining with minimal junctional gaps.
  • Invested with a complete basal lamina
  • Have fenestrations or junctional gaps in between endothelial cells.
  • Accompanied by an incomplete basal lamina
  • Have junctional gaps in the endothelium.
  • Have complete basal lamina
TransportDo not allow ease of transport of diffusible substances to and from the bloodAllows ease of transport and diffusion of substances across the capillaryAllows ease of diffusion but limits the size that crosses the capillary walls
ExamplesCapillaries of the CNS (to maintain the integrity of the BBB)Spleen and liver capillaries lining the sinusoids, and glomerulusCapillaries of the renal glomeruli, intestinal villi, pancreas and endocrine secretory cells
Lecture-Specific Note
  • The trans lists the glomerulus under both discontinuous and fenestrated endothelium.
  • Follow your lecturer’s emphasis if this is asked.

B. Diseases of the Blood Vessels p. 3

  • Congenital anomalies
  • Arteriosclerosis
    • Group of arterial disorders denoting hardening of the arteries
  • Hypertension
  • Vasculitis
    • Diseases involving inflammation of the blood vessels
  • Aneurysms and Dissections
    • Vascular anomalies resulting from abnormal dilation of the blood vessels
  • Pathology of veins and lymphatics
  • Tumors of blood vessels

Vascular Anomalies pp. 3–4

Key PointSome are congenital or developmental in nature, and majority are acquired.

Congenital (Berry) Aneurysm

Definition: Aneurysm = abnormal structural and developmental dilation anomalies of the blood vessels.

  • Often spherical in shape, resembling a fruit berry → “berry aneurysm”
  • Site: commonly at the bifurcation of the blood vessels in the Circle of Willis
    • Muscular wall support is deficient → point of wall weakening → eventual wall dilation through time
  • Risk: potential risk to rupture and cause fatal intracranial hemorrhage

Arterio-Venous Malformation / Fistula

  • Direct communication between arteries and veins, bypassing blood flow along capillaries
    • Arterial blood is directly shunted into the venous system
  • May be congenital, but MOST ARE ACQUIRED
    • Traumatic penetrating injury
    • Iatrogenic causes (surgical AV fistula in hemodialysis)
  • Clinical significance:
    1. Potential risk of hemorrhage
    2. Shunting of blood from arterial to venous system → high output or high volume failure
Take NoteThese arteries and veins do not have networks of capillary connections.

Fibromuscular Dysplasia

  • Definition: Developmental anomaly of the medium-sized and large muscular arteries
    • Common among young to middle-aged women
  • Characterized by:
    • Segmental proliferation
    • Hyperplasia
    • Fibrosis of the intima
    • Media within the arterial wall
  • Consequence:
    Segmental hyperplasia in muscular layer→Thickening of arterial wall→Stenosis→Impaired perfusion → ischemia
    • Renal arteries involved → renovascular hypertension
  • Complications: 1) Aneurysm 2) Dissection 3) Arterial tortuosities
  • Common sites: 1) Renal artery 2) Internal carotid artery 3) Vertebral arteries
Clinical CueString-bead appearance on renal artery angiography = characteristic radiologic feature of fibromuscular dysplasia.
Do Not Confuse
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia is a developmental anomaly (young to middle-aged women, string-bead).
  • Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia is a type of arteriosclerosis caused by iatrogenic mechanisms (stents, angioplasty, AV shunts).
  • See Other Arteriosclerosis tab.

C. Vascular Response to Injury p. 4

  • Studies link endothelial injury to the development of coronary artery disease and ischemic heart disease.
  • The endothelium and other cellular components show normal physiological and pathological responses when exposed to an injurious stimulus.
  • Injurious stimulus may be mechanical, chemical or inflammatory processes that can alter the function and morphology of the blood vessels.

Endothelial Cells

Features

  • Innermost lining of the blood vessel
  • Versatile, multifunctional cells with a wealth of synthetic and metabolic properties
  • Unless injured or otherwise activated, ECs have a non-thrombogenic surface that maintains the blood in a fluid state
  • Play a role in the evolution of important diseases of the arteries like atherosclerosis
  • Elongated to polygonal cells rich in storage organelles and secretions enclosed in pinocytic vesicles
  • Contain Weibel-Palade bodies = storage organelles of vWF
  • Endothelium = highly specialized, metabolically active interface between blood and the underlying tissues
    • Maintains vascular tone
    • Normal laminar flow
    • Thrombo-resistance
    • Selective permeability to cells
    • Proteins

Functions

  • Maintain a permeability barrier
  • Fluid homeostasis and hemostasis (have both pro-coagulant and anti-coagulant activities)
  • Production of ECM
  • Modulation of blood flow
  • Regulation of inflammation and immunity
  • Regulation of cell growth
Endothelial Cell Properties and Functions (Figure 7, Robbins Table 11.1)
Property / FunctionMediators / Products
Maintenance of permeability barrier—
Elaboration of anticoagulant, antithrombotic, and fibrinolytic regulators
  • Prostacyclin

Regulation of cell growth
  • Growth stimulators: PDGF, CSF, FGF
  • Growth inhibitors: heparin, TGF-β

D. Vascular Smooth Muscle Cells p. 4

  • Predominant cellular element of the vascular media
  • Important role in normal vascular repair and healing, such as what is seen in atherosclerosis

Functions

  • Moderation of vascular tone that regulates BP through vasoconstriction and vasodilation
  • Capacity to proliferate when appropriately stimulated
    • Synthesize collagen, elastin and proteoglycans
    • Elaborate growth factors, growth inhibitors and cytokines
  • Migratory and proliferative activity
    • Induced to migrate from its medial location and proliferate in the subendothelium to participate in healing
    • Excessive proliferation → progression of vascular inflammation, plaque formation and atherosclerosis
  • Contractile function

E. Vascular Injury pp. 4–5

May either be acute endothelial cell loss or chronic endothelial injury or dysfunction.

Endothelial Dysfunction

  • Definition: several types of potentially reversible changes in the functional state of endothelial cells that occur in response to environmental stimuli
  • Chronic endothelial injury and dysfunction is implicated in many CVS diseases, particularly atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease
  • ECs exposed to various sub-lethal injurious stimuli → altered structure and function → so-called “neo-intima” or new intima
  • Altered endothelial phenotype is often both pro-inflammatory and pro-thrombogenic

Endothelial Cell Activation

  • Definition: ECs respond to stimuli by adjusting their steady-state functions and expressing newly acquired but inducible properties — a process termed endothelial cell activation
  • Inducers of endothelial activation:
    • Cytokines and bacterial products (elicit inflammation and septic shock in severe cases)
    • Lipids and lipid products
    • Hemodynamic stresses
    • Viruses
    • Complements
    • Nitric oxide
    • Hypoxia
  • Stimulated ECs undergo structural and functional alterations, mediated by elaborated products:
    • Adhesion molecules
    • Procoagulants
    • Pro-inflammatory factors
Basal vs Activated Endothelial Cell (Figure 8)
Basal state“Activated” state
Stimuli
  • Normotension
  • Laminar flow
  • Growth factors (e.g., VEGF)
  • Turbulent flow
  • Hypertension
  • Cytokines
  • Complement
  • Bacterial products
  • Lipid products
  • Advanced glycation end-products
  • Hypoxia
  • Acidosis

  • Cigarette smoke
Endothelial surfaceNon-adhesive, non-thrombogenic surface
  • Increased expression of procoagulants, adhesion molecules and proinflammatory factors
  • Altered expression of chemokines, cytokines and growth factors

F. Intimal Thickening p. 5

  • End result of constant exposure to vascular injury
  • Focal area of exaggerated endothelial healing forming the neo-intima (new intima) from contributions of ECs and SMCs
    • The neo-intima is typically covered by ECs
  • The stereotypical response of the vessel wall to any insult
    • Any injury → healing response involving SMC proliferation, ECM deposition, and intimal expansion
  • Pathologic intimal thickening
    • Represents the earliest lesion of atherosclerosis before progression to fibro-fatty plaques
    • Primarily composed of SMCs near the lumen and ECM of proteoglycan and type III collagen

How it forms

  • Vascular injury with EC dysfunction → SMC recruitment and proliferation with ECM synthesis → intimal thickening that can compromise vascular flow
  • ECs involved in repair migrate from adjacent uninjured areas into injured areas
  • Medial SMCs or circulating smooth muscle precursor cells migrate into the intima, proliferate and synthesize ECM, like fibroblasts fill in a wound
  • Neo-intimal SMCs are regulated by cytokines and growth factors from:
    • Platelets
    • ECs
    • Macrophages
    • Thrombin
    • Activated complement factors
1. Smooth muscle cells migration to the intimacirculating SMCs and SMCs from the medial layer
2. Intimal cell proliferation
3. Synthesis of extracellular matrixcollagen, proteoglycan
Key Differentiator
  • SMCs migrate to the sub-endothelium and become facultative fibroblast-like cells that proliferate and elaborate ECM (collagen, proteoglycan).
  • The resulting intimal SMCs have a proliferative, synthetic, and non-contractile phenotype, distinct from medial SMCs.
ReversibleWith time, the EC layer can be restored and the neo-intimal SMCs can return to a non-proliferative state, so intimal thickening is a reversible phenomenon.

II. Arteriosclerosis — “Hardening of the Arteries” p. 5

Definition: A generic term for arterial wall thickening and loss of elasticity secondary to sclerosis or fibrosis of the arteries.

  • Arteriosclerosis — Types / Patterns
    • Atherosclerosis
    • Mönckeberg Medial Calcific Sclerosis
    • Fibromuscular Intimal Hyperplasia
    • Arteriolosclerosis
      • Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
      • Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis

A. Patterns of Arteriosclerosis — Atherosclerosis pp. 5–6

Atherosclerosis Must Know

  • Arteries are hardened due to deposits of basic lesions of intimal atheroma or fibro-fatty plaques
  • Can be considered a chronic inflammatory response of the intima initiated by exposure of the endothelium to various injurious conditions
  • Characterized by deposition of intimal fibrous plaques that often have a central core that is rich in lipid
  • Underlies the pathogenesis of coronary, cerebral, and peripheral vascular disease

Predilection

InvolvedExamples
Large elastic arteriesAorta, carotid and iliac arteries
Large medium-sized muscular arteriesCoronary, renal, and popliteal arteries
NOT involvedArterioles and small muscular arteries
Exam Trap
  • Atherosclerosis does not involve the arterioles and small muscular arteries.
  • From the plenary quiz feedback: “Atheroma does not develop in small end arterioles.” A small-arteriole lesion in a diabetic / hypertensive patient points to hyaline arteriolosclerosis, not atheroma.

B. Diseases Associated with Atherosclerosis p. 6

These account for more than half of the annual mortality in the United States and western countries:

  • Ischemic heart disease
    • Leading cause of death (subsequently declined by more than 30%)
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Cerebrovascular accident (CVA) or stroke
  • Infarction (or gangrene) of extremities
  • Infarction of GIT
  • Abdominal aortic aneurysm

C. Risk Factors in Atherosclerosis pp. 6–7

Classification of Risk Factors
CategoryLecture definition
Major risk factorsDue to the high association in its development and pathogenesis of the disease
Minor risk factorsDue to some contribution to risk development, albeit at a lower, less defined level
Controllable risk factorsCan be altered by treatment or lifestyle modification
Non-modifiable / constitutionalCannot be altered because they are part of the inherent make up or constituent of the person

Major Modifiable Risk Factors

1. Hyperlipidemia or High Fat Diet Must Know

  • Lipid, particularly its oxidized form, is known to injure endothelial cells
    • Basic building block of atheroma or fibro-fatty plaque
    • Major component: Cholesterol (LDL, VLDL, IDL, triglycerides, and chylomicrons)
  • High blood lipid → insudation of lipid into the intima and sub-intima → becomes the core substance of the fibro-fatty plaque
  • One of the most important risk factors in the etiopathogenesis of atherosclerosis
  • Lipoprotein density: the higher the lipid content, the lower the density. The higher the protein, the more dense and heavy the LP.
  • LDL – “bad cholesterol”
    • Major component of total cholesterol
    • Has a direct positive correlation to the development of atherosclerosis and its associated diseases (e.g. AMI and CVA)
  • Hyperlipidemia and dyslipoproteinemias may result from:
    • Genetic mutations involving genes for apolipoproteins
    • Other underlying disorders:
      • Nephrotic syndrome
      • Alcoholism
      • Hypothyroidism
      • DM

2. Cigarette Smoking

  • Nicotine, benzene, polyaromatic hydrocarbon are endotheliotoxic → damage the endothelial intimal cells
  • Prolonged smoking of one pack or more per day increases the death rate from CAD and IHD by 200%

3. Hypertension

  • Increases the risk of IHD by approximately 60% vs normotensive individuals, particularly when HPN occurs after 45 years of age
  • BP exceeding 169/90 mmHg → more than 5-fold greater risk of IHD vs BP of 140/90 mmHg or lower

4. Diabetes Mellitus

  • Associated with hypercholesterolemia, with a markedly increased predisposition to atherosclerosis
  • Incidence of myocardial infarction is twice as high in a diabetic vs a nondiabetic individual

Major Non-Modifiable Risk Factors

1. Age

  • 5x increase from those aged 40–60 years old
    • Atherosclerotic plaque development is a progressive process, usually clinically manifested during middle age
    • Between ages 40 and 60, incidence of AMI with underlying coronary atherosclerosis increases fivefold
    • Death rates from IHD rise with each decade

2. Male Gender

  • Males have higher risk because of lifestyle and behavior typically associated with males, like cigarette smoking
  • Pre-menopausal females have lower incidence, as estrogen has cardio-protective and vasculo-protective properties

3. Genetic Abnormalities: Familial Hypercholesterolemia

  • Family history is the most important independent risk factor for development of atherosclerosis
  • May involve mendelian disorders of familial hypercholesterolemia

4. Polygenic Familial History

  • Disease clusters like DM, HPN, which may be transmitted genetically within family members

Other Minor Risk Factors p. 7

  • Inflammation
  • Metabolic syndrome: Obesity
    • A group of factors that raises the risk for:
      • Heart disease
      • Atherosclerosis
      • DM
      • Stroke
    • Risk factors:
      • Large waistline (abdominal obesity)
      • High triglyceride levels
      • Low HDL levels
      • High BP
      • High FBS
    • Provides the setting for development of hyperlipidemia, DM, and HPN
  • Physical inactivity
  • Type A personality / stress
    • Outgoing
    • Competitive
    • Ambitious
    • Rigidly organized
    • Impatient
    • Anxious
    • Frequently stressed

  • High CHO, unsaturated fat intake, alcohol

    • Correlated with CAD, PVD, stroke, or venous thrombosis

Value Box — Risk Numbers
  • Smoking ≥ 1 pack/day (prolonged) → death rate from CAD and IHD ↑ 200%
  • HPN → IHD risk ↑ about 60%, particularly when HPN occurs after 45 years
  • BP > 169/90 mmHg → > 5-fold greater IHD risk vs ≤ 140/90 mmHg
  • DM → MI incidence twice as high
  • Age 40–60 → AMI incidence ↑ fivefold
Exam Trap
  • Age is a non-modifiable risk factor.
  • Diabetes mellitus, cigarette smoking and hypertension are modifiable.

D. Pathogenesis — Hypotheses p. 7

HypothesisKey ideaStatus
1. Response to InjuryAtherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory response of the arterial wall to various forms of endothelial injury, leading to endothelial dysfunctionWidespread acceptance as the primary mechanism
2. Monoclonal
  • Focused on smooth muscle proliferation.
  • SMCs forming the fibrous caps migrate from the underlying media, then proliferate.
  • Lesions arise as an aberration of growth control in one type of cell, similar to a benign smooth muscle tumor (e.g. leiomyoma)
Debunked: proliferation involves multiple clones of cells from macrophages, leukocytes, platelets, etc.
3. Organization and Growth of Thrombi—Not generally accepted
4. Infection—Not generally accepted

Response to Injury Hypothesis p. 7

Must Know — Summary of the Model
  • Atherosclerosis = a chronic inflammatory and healing response of the arterial wall in response to endothelial injury.
  • The healing response is the formation of the neo-intima.
  • Lesion progression occurs through interaction of modified lipoproteins, monocyte-derived macrophages, and T lymphocytes with ECs and SMCs of the arterial wall.
  • Endothelial injury and dysfunction cause intimal proliferation from smooth muscle migration and proliferation with lipid insudation.
  • The SM proliferation heals the injured intima by elaboration of ECM, similar to the wound healing process.
  • Can be triggered by any number of insults, alone or in combination
    • Physical injury
    • Stress
    • Trauma
    • Hypertension
    • Turbulent flow
    • Hyperlipidemia
    • Cigarette smoking
    • Carbohydrate excess, etc.
  • Intimal proliferation is a reaction to insudation of lipids

Roles of Each Player pp. 7–8

Role of Endothelial Injury Must Know

  • EC injury is the cornerstone of the response to injury hypothesis
  • Early lesions begin at sites of morphologically intact endothelium that exhibits endothelial dysfunction:
    • Increased endothelial cell permeability
    • Enhanced leukocyte adhesions
    • Altered gene expression
  • Causes of EC injury:
    • HPN
    • Irradiation
    • Chemical toxins like lipid, nicotine
    • Immune complex deposition
    • Turbulence flow and hemodynamic disturbance
  • Endothelial dysfunction includes toxins from cigarette smoke, homocysteine, and local inflammatory cytokines
Three Most Important Causes of Endothelial Dysfunction
  1. Hemodynamic disturbances
  2. Hypercholesterolemia
  3. Inflammation

Role of Lipid

  • Impairs endothelial function → production of superoxide and O₂ free radicals
  • Lipid accumulation at the site of injury
  • Dyslipoproteinemias: lipoprotein abnormalities characterized by increased LDL, decreased HDL, and increased levels of abnormal Lipoprotein A
    • Caused by genetic abnormalities in apoproteins or lipoprotein receptors, or other disorders:
      • Nephrotic syndrome
      • Alcoholism
      • Hypothyroidism
      • Diabetes mellitus
    • All are associated with an increased risk of atherosclerosis
  • Evidence implicating hyperlipidemia / hypercholesterolemia:
    • Structural: presence of cholesterols in the core of fibro-fatty plaque at the site of injury
    • Epidemiologic: direct correlation of atherosclerosis with high levels of blood cholesterol

The oxidized form of LDL plays roles in:

Effect of oxidized LDL
Formation of foam cells
Increased adhesion of monocytes
Increased chemotaxis to circulating monocytes
Inhibition of the mobility of macrophages
Stimulation of release of growth factors
Endotheliotoxic

Role of Macrophages

  • Inflammation of the vessel wall from whatever cause (bacteria, virus, chemical toxins from lipid and nicotine) can trigger atherogenesis
Inciting event→Inflammasome activation in macrophages→Proinflammatory cytokine IL-1→Recruits and activates macrophages and T lymphocytes

The activated macrophages and T lymphocytes produce locally:

  • Local cytokines, chemokines and TNF → recruit and activate more inflammatory cells
  • Reactive oxygen species → enhance LDL oxidation
  • Growth factors → drive SMC proliferation

Role of Smooth Muscle

  • Significant role through: SMC proliferation and ECM synthesis
  • Intimal SMC proliferation and ECM deposition convert a fatty streak into a mature atheroma (fibro-fatty plaque) and contribute to the progressive growth of lesions
  • Growth factors: PDGF, FGF, and TGF-α
    • Also stimulate SMCs to synthesize ECM, notably collagen, which stabilizes the atherosclerotic plaque

Events of Atherogenesis pp. 8–10

  1. Chronic endothelial injury
    • Altered state of endothelial dysfunction → permeable intimal state, favoring insudation of circulating LPs
    • Under normal conditions, leukocytes do NOT adhere to ECs
    • After damage, ECs produce adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 → monocytes and T lymphocytes adhere to the endothelium and migrate beneath it by squeezing between the ECs
    • Monocytes and T cells are attracted by chemoattractant cytokines and chemokines
    • ECs change in shape and tight junctions loosen up → ↑ permeability to fluid, lipids, and leukocytes
  2. Insudation of lipoproteins into vessel wall
    • Lipoprotein particles, especially LDL, enter the arterial wall and undergo oxidation
    • Oxidation results from exposure to nitric oxide, macrophages, and enzymes such as lipoxygenase
    • Lipid and other stimuli release proinflammatory factors like cytokines (interleukin)
  3. Adhesion / migration of monocytes into the intima → macrophages / foam cells
    • Monocytes differentiate into macrophages and take up oxidized LDL
    • Lipid-laden macrophage = foam cell
    • Foam cells undergo apoptosis, but lipid progressively accumulates in the intima as a yellow lipid grumous core
  4. Platelet adhesion to the injured site
    • Platelets liberate PDGF, FGF, TGF-α, which stimulate intimal migration of the smooth muscle
  5. Intimal migration of SMCs
    • Macrophages, T lymphocytes and platelets secrete growth factors, principally PDGF, FGF, and TGF-α → stimulate smooth muscle recruitment
    • SMCs may originate from circulating smooth muscle, but mostly from the tunica media
  6. Proliferation of SM cells and elaboration of ECM
    • Primarily Collagen III and proteoglycan deposition
    • ECM is an important building block of the basic lesion, together with insudation and accumulation of lipids
  7. Lipid accumulation, fibrous deposition → fibro-fatty plaque / atheroma formation
    • Fibro-fatty plaque: a central core of lipid surrounded by fibrous tissue containing foam macrophages, leukocytes and lymphocytes
  • Injury triggers monocyte adhesion and loosening of EC junctions → migration of monocytes beneath
  • Permeable endothelium lets LDL and cholesterol enter the intima
  • Macrophages engulf LDL by phagocytosis → foam cells
  • T-lymphocytes within the intima secrete cytokines that induce SMCs to migrate from media to intima
  • SMCs proliferate under growth factors → progressive accumulation of lipids and SMCs in the intima → lesion raises the endothelium and encroaches on the lumen
  • This begins to transform a fatty streak into a fibro-fatty nodule
Must Know — Lecturer Emphasis (red text)
  • Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory response of the arterial wall, initiated by some form of endothelial damage.
  • Endothelial dysfunction is a state of altered structure and function of the endothelium that allows for:
    • Increased permeability of the intima
    • Intimal adhesion of monocytes, leukocytes, and platelets
High-Yield Recap
  • Extracellular lipid, foam cells and scattered T-lymphocytes in the subendothelium → fatty streak, the earliest precursor lesion.
  • With progression of endothelial damage, the fatty streak is transformed into atheroma or fibro-fatty plaque, the basic lesion.
  • Atheroma:
    • Central core of lipids
    • Surrounded by foam cells and leukocytes (primarily T-lymphocytes)
    • ECM of collagen
    • Covered by a fibrous cap

E. Morphology of Atherosclerosis — Fatty Streak p. 10

❗ Must KnowFatty streak = Precursor lesion of atherosclerosis.

Fatty Streak Must Know

  • May occur early in NB, children, or at birth
  • Does not cause any disturbance in blood flow
  • No clinical significance

Gross

  • Multiple flat, yellow spots or streaks (fatty dots), <1 mm in diameter on the intimal surface
  • Fatty dots = minute, millimeter-sized, pearly white to yellow dots in the intima that merge into an elongated, 1 cm long linear lesion = fatty streaks

Microscopic

  • Aggregates of lipid foam cells with scattering T-lymphocytes and extracellular lipids

Atheroma p. 11

❗ Must Know
  • Basic lesion: atheroma / fibro-fatty plaque / fibro-lipid plaque
  • Focal intimal plaque with central core of lipid and covering fibrous cap
  • Atherosclerosis has predilection for certain arteries.
  • It affects the:
    • Abdominal aorta
    • Coronary artery
    • Popliteal artery
    • Descending thoracic aorta
    • Internal carotid artery
    • Arteries of the Circle of Willis

Gross Features

  • Normal flat, smooth intimal surface of the aorta is transformed by deposits of atheromas → varied sized nodular yellow elevations in the intima
  • White to yellow and produce raised protruding nodules into the lumen
  • The center of a larger plaque may contain yellow debris, hence the term atheroma
  • Abdominal aorta is usually more involved than the thoracic aorta
  • Aortic lesions are more prominent around the origins of its major branches

Microscopic Features

  • Initially covered by an endothelial fibrous cap and tend to involve the intima
  • Central core of lipids surrounded by dense sclerotic ECM, with scattered foam macrophages and lymphocytes, covered by a fibrous cap
  • Central core contains:
    • Smooth muscle
    • Macrophages
    • Lymphocytes
    • Lipid laden cells (foam cells)
    • ECM
  • Central core also contains necrotic debris. Cholesterol crystals and foreign body giant cells may be present within the fibrous tissue and necrotic areas.
  • Foam cells represent both macrophages and smooth muscle cells that have taken up lipids
  • Numerous inflammatory and immune cells, especially T-cells, are present within the plaque
Essential Components of an Atheroma (3 principal components)
ComponentContents
CellsSmooth muscle, macrophages, leukocytes (T-lymphocytes)
Connective tissue ECMCollagen, elastic fibers, proteoglycans
Intra and extracellular lipidCholesterol and cholesterol esters
  • Extracellularly: clear spaces simulating needle clefts and irregular globoid-shaped clear spaces
  • Intracellularly: within the cytoplasm of macrophages (foam cells)
Definition to Memorize
  • Atheroma is an intimal lesion with a core of lipid (mainly cholesterol and cholesterol esters) and a covering fibrous cap.
  • In advanced atherosclerosis, the fatty atheroma may be converted into a fibrous scar.
Recognition Cue
  • H&E: extracellular lipids appear as needle cleft spaces or irregular-sized globules of clear spaces, because fat was dissolved during tissue processing.
  • Special fat stain: Sudan or Oil red-O yields a magenta-red color.

From Precursor to Complicated Lesion p. 12

Fatty streakprecursor lesion
Fibro-fatty plaque / atheromabasic lesion of atherosclerosis
Complicated atheromatous plaquewhen injurious stimuli are not mitigated

F. Complicated Lesions of Atherosclerosis pp. 12–14

Definition: Basic lesions (i.e. atheroma) that are secondarily complexed by superimposed lesions.

Defined by the presence of:
Complicated lesionMechanism / lecture detailConsequence
CalcificationPatchy or massive calcificationArtery stenosis, ischemia and peripheral vascular disease
Focal rupture, gross ulceration, or erosionPlaques rupture when unable to withstand mechanical stresses generated by vascular shear forces. Triggered by:
  • Intrinsic factors: plaque structure and composition
  • Extrinsic factors: blood pressure, platelet reactivity, and vessel spasm
Exposes the intima to highly thrombogenic substances → thrombus
Thrombus formation and cholesterol embolizationDue to exposure of the bloodstream to highly thrombogenic substances arising from the rupture, ulceration, or erosion of the plaque surface
  • Downstream ischemia and infarction (partial or complete occlusion)
  • Discharge of debris → microemboli (atheroembolism)
Hemorrhage into a plaqueRupture of overlying fibrous cap or thin-walled vessels of neovascularization → intraplaque hemorrhage—
AneurysmDilatation due to weakening of the blood vessel wall
  • Potential rupture and hemorrhage
  • Commonly seen in abdominal aortic aneurysm

Vulnerable vs Stable Plaque p. 13

  • The fibrous cap undergoes continuous remodeling that can stabilize it or render it more susceptible to rupture
  • The balance between collagen synthesis and degradation affects cap integrity
    • Collagen = major structural component of the fibrous cap, accounts for its mechanical strength and stability
Vulnerable plaqueStable plaque
Fibrous capThin fibrous capsThick, densely collagenous fibrous caps
Lipid coreLarge lipid coresUnderlying atheromatous core
InflammationIncreased inflammationMinimal inflammation
BehaviorMore likely to ruptureMore stable

Clinical Consequences p. 14

  • Rupture, ulceration, or erosion of a plaque exposes the intima to highly thrombogenic substances and induces thrombus formation, further occluding the lumen
    • → downstream blood flow obstruction and ischemia
    • Seen in Acute Myocardial Infarction and thrombotic CVA with brain infarct and gangrene
  • Aneurysm formation from weakening of the blood vessel wall → potential rupture and hemorrhage
  • Embolic phenomenon from dislodgement of cholesterol material into the bloodstream
  • Disease associated with atherosclerosis:
    • Ischemic heart disease
    • CVA
    • Gangrene of extremities, intestine
    • Abdominal aortic aneurysm
❗ Key Features of Atherosclerosis
  • Etiological agents produce endothelial injury and dysfunction → initially fatty streak → develops into atheroma → progresses into complicated atherosclerotic plaques.
  • Calcification can lead to artery stenosis, ischemia and peripheral vascular disease.
Complications Tree (Figure 31)
CalcificationRuptureHemorrhageEmbolization (distal sites)Aneurysm
  • Renal artery stenosis
  • Angina
  • Peripheral vascular disease
  • Myocardial infarction
  • Thrombotic stroke
—Embolic strokeAAA
Exam Trap
  • The basic lesion of atherosclerosis is the fibro-fatty plaque only.
  • Ulcerated atheroma and calcified atheroma are complicated lesions, not basic lesions.
  • A fatty streak is not dangerous, not prone to ischemia, and not associated with advanced atherosclerosis.
  • It is a lesion that may progress.

III. Other Types of Arteriosclerosis p. 14

  • “Hardening of arteries” — other types
    • Mönckeberg Medial Calcific Sclerosis
    • Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia (medium muscular arteries)
    • Arteriolosclerosis (small-end arterioles)
      • Hyaline arteriolosclerosis
      • Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis

A. Mönckeberg’s Medial Calcific Sclerosis (MMCS) pp. 14–15

MMCS Must Know

  • Definition: arteries hardened because of plate-like calcifications involving the tunica media
  • Degenerative and non-inflammatory calcification of the media of large and medium-sized muscular arteries
    • Most often involves arteries of the upper and lower extremities
  • Occurs principally in:
    • Older persons (>50 years of age)
    • Diabetics and those with chronic renal disease
  • Calcification is dystrophic in nature
  • Clinically, the calcified vessel is described as “pipe stem” due to rigid hardening from medial calcification
  • Prone to develop secondary atherosclerosis
Must Know
  • This lesion has NO clinical significance and DOES NOT produce obstruction.
  • Why: it involves the media, and the intima is not involved.
Lecture NoteObstruction may happen if the patient develops secondary atherosclerosis because of damaged intimal cells.

From synchronous lecture feedback

  • Affects medium-sized muscular arteries
  • Hardened because of plaque-like calcific deposit of the media of the artery
  • Degenerative process, commonly seen in aging populations
  • Particularly affected: patients with Diabetes Mellitus
Exam Trap
  • For MMCS, “common complication is vascular occlusion and ischemia” is the INCORRECT statement.
  • Correct: associated with aging and DM, occurs in medium-sized muscular arteries, prone to superimposed atherosclerosis.
  • Plate-like calcifications = MMCS.

B. Fibromuscular Intimal Hyperplasia p. 15

Fibromuscular Intimal Hyperplasia

  • Caused by iatrogenic mechanisms
  • Arteries hardened due to fibrosis and hyperplasia of the tunica intima and media as a response to inflammation and mechanical injury
  • Occurs in medium-sized muscular arteries
  • Defined by the presence of:
    • Inflammation (e.g. healed arteritis or transplant-associated arteriopathy)
    • Mechanical injury from iatrogenic procedures (e.g. stents or balloon angioplasty, hemodialysis AV shunts)
  • Considered a healing process / response of the blood vessels to inflammation and mechanical trauma
  • Characteristics:
    • Vessel fibrosis and stenosis due to hyperplasia of the tunica media and intima, principally contributed by the smooth muscle cells
    • Inflammation may also be present
Fibrosis→Stenosis→Occlusion→Ischemia
Clinical Cue
  • Associated with in-stent restenosis.
  • It is the major long-term limitation of solid organ transplants.

C. Arteriolosclerosis pp. 15–16

Affects very small-end arteries or arterioles, hence the name “arteriolosclerosis”. Two types:

Hyaline arteriolosclerosisHyperplastic arteriolosclerosis (onion skin)
Why hardenedDeposits in the media of pink, acellular hyaline substanceHyperplasia or proliferation of the intima and medial cells of the arterioles
HypertensionBenign hypertension (mild to moderate increase in BP)Malignant (accelerated) hypertension: very high elevation, with diastolic hypertension (vs only systolic hypertension in benign)
Other associationsOld age and diabetes mellitus—
Pathogenesis / pathologyLeakage of plasma components across endothelium (from fibrin) into the media, deposited as hyaline material (with hyaline deposition by SM)Concentric lamination of arterioles from proliferation of intima and media → “onion skinning”, progressive narrowing of lumen
MorphologyHyaline pink, glassy deposits in media of small arteriolesOnion skinning: concentric laminated thickening of media
OutcomeLeads to end-stage nephrosclerosisAssociated fibrinoid necrosis of the intima → necrotizing arteriolitis
Clinical Cue
  • A 50-year-old woman with type 2 DM and hypertension with renal biopsy for chronic renal disease → hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
  • Clue: pink homogenous deposits + old age, DM, HPN.

Cram Sheet

❗ Red-Mark Must Knows (lecture wording)
  • Fatty streak → Precursor lesion of atherosclerosis
  • Atheroma → The basic lesion of atherosclerosis.
  • Also called fibro-fatty plaque / fibro-lipid plaque
  • Focal intimal plaque with central core of lipid and covering fibrous cap
  • Predilection:
    • Abdominal aorta
    • Coronary artery
    • Popliteal artery
    • Descending thoracic aorta
    • Internal carotid artery
    • Arteries of the Circle of Willis
  • Key features: risk factors → atherosclerosis development and progression → complications:
    • Calcification
    • Rupture
    • Hemorrhage
    • Embolization
    • Aneurysm

Core Definitions

  • Arteriosclerosis: generic term for arterial wall thickening and loss of elasticity secondary to sclerosis or fibrosis (“hardening of the arteries”)
  • Atherosclerosis: chronic inflammatory response of the intima initiated by exposure of the endothelium to injurious conditions
    • Intimal fibrous plaques with a lipid-rich central core
  • Endothelial dysfunction: potentially reversible changes in EC functional state in response to environmental stimuli
    • Allows ↑ permeability of the intima and intimal adhesion of monocytes, leukocytes, and platelets
  • Endothelial cell activation: ECs express newly acquired but inducible properties
  • Intimal thickening: stereotypical response to any insult → SMC proliferation, ECM deposition, intimal expansion (neo-intima)
    • Pathologic intimal thickening = earliest lesion before fibro-fatty plaque. Reversible.
  • Complicated lesion: atheroma secondarily complexed by superimposed lesions

Atherogenesis Sequence

Chronic endothelial injury→↑ permeability + VCAM-1→LDL insudation + oxidation→Monocytes → macrophages → foam cells→Fatty streak→Platelets / macrophages / T cells release PDGF, FGF, TGF-α→SMC migration (mostly from media)→SMC proliferation + Collagen III, proteoglycan→Atheroma / fibro-fatty plaque→Complicated plaque
  • EC injury is the cornerstone of the response to injury hypothesis (the accepted primary mechanism)
  • Top 3 causes of endothelial dysfunction: hemodynamic disturbances, hypercholesterolemia, inflammation
  • Leukocytes do NOT adhere to normal ECs
  • LDL oxidation: by nitric oxide, macrophages, lipoxygenase
  • Inflammasome → IL-1 → recruits macrophages and T cells → cytokines/TNF, ROS (↑ LDL oxidation), growth factors (SMC proliferation)
  • SMC-made collagen stabilizes the plaque

Oxidized LDL — Six Roles

CellsEffect
Foam cellsFormation
Monocytes↑ adhesion and ↑ chemotaxis
MacrophagesInhibits mobility
Growth factorsStimulates release
EndotheliumEndotheliotoxic

PartContents
CellsSmooth muscle, macrophages, T-lymphocytes
ECMCollagen, elastic fibers, proteoglycans
LipidCholesterol and cholesterol esters: extracellular (needle clefts) and intracellular (foam cells)
CoreNecrotic debris, cholesterol crystals, foreign body giant cells
Foam cellsBoth macrophages and SMCs that took up lipid
  • Abdominal aorta more involved than thoracic. Lesions prominent at origins of major branches.
  • Advanced: fatty atheroma may become a fibrous scar.

Common Exam Traps
  • Atheroma does not develop in small end arterioles.
  • Atherosclerosis spares arterioles and small muscular arteries.
  • Basic lesion = fibro-fatty plaque only.
  • Ulcerated and calcified atheromas are complicated.
  • Fatty streak causes no flow disturbance and has no clinical significance.
  • Age is non-modifiable.
  • DM, smoking and HPN are modifiable.
  • MMCS does NOT cause occlusion and ischemia, unless secondary atherosclerosis develops.
  • Family history is the most important independent risk factor.
  • Monoclonal hypothesis is debunked.
  • Response to injury is the accepted primary mechanism.
  • AVM: may be congenital, but most are acquired.
Do Not Confuse
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia (developmental anomaly, string-bead) vs fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia (iatrogenic arteriosclerosis, in-stent restenosis).
  • Medial SMCs (contractile) vs intimal SMCs (proliferative, synthetic, non-contractile).
  • Benign HPN → hyaline vs malignant HPN → hyperplastic.
